say: Today you are architects. Architects plan rooms, gardens and fences, so they need two numbers: how much space is inside (the area) and how long the edge is (the perimeter).
Here is a puzzle to keep in your head: can two gardens have the same fence but different amounts of grass? Let us find out.
When I read a job, show me with your hand. If the job goes round the edge, trace a finger round the edge in the air: perimeter. If the job covers the inside, wipe your flat palm: area.
Ready? Job 1: put a fence round a garden.
You have 12 squares. You must use all of them to make a rectangle. Will every rectangle you make have the same perimeter? Thumbs up for yes, down for no. Write your guess on your whiteboard.
stuck: Stuck: put 2 squares in each row. How many rows do you need for 12?
Not sure how to find the perimeter: run your finger round the edge and count every side of a square you pass.
Ready for more: can you make a rectangle with 12 squares that has a perimeter of 20 cm? (No: the perimeters are 26, 16 and 14 cm.)

say: “Ravi has 20 m of fence. Half of it goes along one length and one width, so length + width = 10. I list in order: width 1, length 9; width 2, length 8; and so on. I stop at 5 and 5, because after that the rectangles just turn round.”
“This staircase has short steps with no numbers. I do not need them! I push the top pieces up and the side pieces out. Now it is a rectangle with the same perimeter: 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 cm.”
“For the area of an L-shape I cut it into two rectangles. Then I check another way: I fill in the missing corner and take it away. Both ways give 42 cm², so I trust my answer.”

do: Ask: “Is that the area or the perimeter? Which unit goes with it?”
Ask: “How do you know you have found every rectangle?”
Ask: “Can you push the steps out? Is there a dent?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw it on the grid and count.”
Hint 2: “Half the perimeter is one length plus one width.”
Hint 3: “Cut the shape into rectangles. Find each area, then add.”

say: “Two gardens have the same perimeter. Must they have the same area? Show me an example.”
“When does pushing out the steps NOT work?”
ask: “Two gardens have the same perimeter. Must they have the same area? Show me an example.”
No. A 9 m by 1 m garden and a 5 m by 5 m garden both have a 20 m fence, but the areas are 9 m² and 25 m². Pushing out does not work when the shape has a dent: the two walls of the dent are extra.

say: “You listed in order so nothing was missed, and you changed the shape to make it easy. Real architects do the same. Well done!”

p3l7-title.note: Objective: Find the area and perimeter of figures made of squares and rectangles, list every rectangle with a given perimeter in order, and change the shape (push the steps out; cut it up or fill it in) to find perimeters and areas quickly. Heuristics taught today: (1) make a list in order, (2) change the shape. Materials: 12 square tiles (or 12 squares cut from 1 cm grid paper) per child, 1 cm grid paper, mini whiteboards, a ruler. Online: children cut 12 squares from squared paper (or draw on squared paper) and hold their rectangles up to the camera; annotate the grid slides with the pen tool. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 5 to 8 (two rounds) and three quick questions 8 to 11, explore 11 to 24.5 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 24.5 to 36 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36 to 41, worksheet 41 to 72 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 69 everyone chooses), talk time 72 to 79 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 79 to 85, look back 85 to 88, stamp and close 88 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it.

p3l7-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "show me" ONCE for both: children hold up their paper with both answers in one camera hold-up (about 30 seconds). SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and show them only to the tutor on camera (or everybody holds paper to the camera at the same moment, once for both puzzles). No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): Area 6 cm², perimeter 10 cm. Listen for: 6 squares cover it. Walk round the edge: 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): Yes, e.g. 26 cm and 16 cm. Listen for: 1 by 12 has perimeter 26 cm; 2 by 6 has 16 cm; 3 by 4 has 14 cm. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l7-warm1.note: Minutes 5 to 8. Everyone stands. Read each job aloud. Children show with their hands: trace a finger round an imaginary edge for perimeter, wipe a flat palm across for area. Then click to show the answer (clicks reveal jobs 1 to 6 in order). Answers: 1 fence: perimeter. 2 tiles: area. 3 ribbon round the edge: perimeter. 4 paint: area. 5 frame: perimeter. 6 cover a book: area. Ask each time: "Does the job go ROUND the edge, or does it COVER the inside?" Ready for more: "Which unit would you use for the fence: m or m²? For the tiles?" (m for the fence, m² for the floor). Watch for children who think a frame is area because it is a flat thing: it only goes round the edge.

p3l7-warm2.note: Minutes 8 to 11. Whiteboards. Read each question, give thinking time, then click to show the answer. Answers: 1) 56 2) 24 cm (6 + 6 + 6 + 6, or 4 × 6) 3) 24 cm² (8 × 3). Three quick questions only; the square-root question (a square has an area of 49 cm²: each side 7 cm) is on the take-home box of the Go further page in the workbook. Ask after 2 and 3: "Both answers are 24. Are they the same?" No: 24 cm is a length round the edge; 24 cm² is 24 squares of space inside. Check every child writes cm² for an area.

p3l7-explore1.note: Minutes 11 to 20.5. Pairs (or each child online) build rectangles with exactly 12 squares (1 by 12, 2 by 6 and 3 by 4: three rectangles) and record them in the 3-row table on a whiteboard or squared paper (about 6 minutes of pair work). Predict first: "Will every rectangle have the same perimeter?" Remind: a rectangle turned round is the same rectangle. Hints: "Put 2 squares in each row. How many rows?" "Run your finger round the edge and count every side you pass." Ready for more: "Can you make a 12-square rectangle with a perimeter of 20 cm?" (No.) Online: cut squares from squared paper, or just draw the rectangles on squared paper. GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): 16 squares: make every rectangle. Which has the longest perimeter? The shortest? Answer: 16 squares: 1 by 16 (perimeter 34 cm), 2 by 8 (20 cm), 4 by 4 (16 cm). Longest 1 by 16, shortest 4 by 4: the square, the most compact shape. Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l7-explore2.note: Minutes 20.5 to 24.5. Let pairs keep working, then gather the group. Make a class table in order: 1 by 12, 2 by 6, 3 by 4. Answers: 1) 3 rectangles (12 by 1, 6 by 2, 4 by 3; turning one round does not make a new one). 2) No: 26 cm, 16 cm and 14 cm. Same area, different perimeters! 3) The long thin 12 by 1: when squares are in a long line, fewer of their sides touch, so more sides are on the outside. The fattest one (4 by 3, closest to a square) has the shortest perimeter. Ask: "How do you know you have them all?" (We tried 1 row, 2 rows, 3 rows; 4 rows is the 3 by 4 turned round; 5 rows does not work.) That is listing in order: today's first heuristic.

p3l7-teach1.note: Teach heuristic 1: make a list in order. Click 1: half the fence. Ask: "Why half?" (The fence goes length, width, length, width: one length and one width is half of it.) Clicks 2 to 6: build the table row by row; children call out each row. Click 7: the stop rule. Click 8: the answer. Think-aloud: "If I guess gardens at random I might miss one or write one twice. So I start with width 1 and go up by 1 each time. When width and length are both 5 I stop, because 6 and 4 is just 4 and 6 turned round." Point at the Area column: "Same fence, but the areas go 9, 16, 21, 24, 25. The closer to a square, the bigger the area." This is a parallel example: the worksheet uses 18 m.

p3l7-try1.note: Whiteboards together, then click. a) Length + width = 6: 5 and 1, 4 and 2, 3 and 3. That is 3 rectangles. b) Areas 5, 8, 9 cm²: the 3 by 3 square is biggest. c) Length + width = 7: list 6 and 1 (area 6), 5 and 2 (10), 4 and 3 (12). So 4 cm and 3 cm. Ask a child to explain how the list helped in c.

p3l7-teach2.note: Teach heuristic 2: change the shape. Ask first: "What is the perimeter?" Let them count. Click 1: the 12 edges numbered (walk round with your finger). Click 2: the red arrows slide each step piece out to the dashed square. Click 3: same lengths, so same perimeter as the 3 by 3 square. Think-aloud: "Counting edges works, but it is slow and I can lose my place. When a shape goes down in steps, I can push the steps out. The pieces facing up slide up and make the top. The pieces facing right slide right and make the right side. Nothing gets longer or shorter, so the perimeter is the same as the big square." Click 4: the warning about dents (we test it in Your turn c). This is a parallel example: the worksheet staircase has 4 steps.

p3l7-try2.note: Worked example and your turn in one slide (the old separate worked-example slide was merged here). First show the method with a staircase whose steps have no numbers (8 cm wide, 6 cm tall): the pieces facing up slide to the top and together are as long as the bottom, 8 cm; the pieces facing right slide to the side and together are as tall as the left side, 6 cm; perimeter 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 cm. "I do not need the step lengths." Then whiteboards, then click. a) Push out: a 7 by 4 rectangle, 7 + 4 + 7 + 4 = 22 cm, whatever the steps are. b) A cut corner pushes out: still 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 cm (the area drops to 32 cm², but the perimeter stays the same!). c) A dent: pushing out gives 24 cm, but the dent has two walls of 2 cm inside it, so 24 + 2 + 2 = 28 cm. Ask: "Why are b and c different?" In b the cut pieces face out and slide out; in c the two walls of the dent face each other and cannot slide anywhere.

p3l7-teach3.note: Teach: change the shape for area. First ask: "Which sides do we know? Which are missing?" (The step is 3 cm across, 8 − 5, and 2 cm down, 6 − 4.) Click 1: cut along the red line into a 5 by 6 and a 3 by 4 rectangle. Click 2: the second way: fill in the corner to make an 8 by 6 rectangle, then take the corner away. Click 3: both give 42. Think-aloud: "I cannot find the area of an L-shape in one go, so I change it into rectangles. I can cut it up, or fill it in and take away. If both ways give the same answer, I know I am right." Also ask: "What is its perimeter?" (Push out: 8 + 6 + 8 + 6 = 28 cm.) Parallel example: the worksheet L-shape is 10 cm by 7 cm.

p3l7-key.note: Say the key ideas together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Mixing up area and perimeter, or writing cm for an area (it is cm²). (2) Counting squares along the edge instead of edges for perimeter: a corner square has 2 edges on the outside, so count edges, not squares. (3) Pushing out a shape with a dent and forgetting the dent's two walls. (4) In Q2, listing a garden twice (5 by 4 and 4 by 5) or missing one because the list is not in order. (5) Finding the missing sides of the L-shape wrongly: take away, do not add.

p3l7-break.note: Five minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p3l7-teachsq.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3 asks the same kind of question with different numbers). Click through the steps. Ask before step 2: "What do we know about the sides of a square?" (all 4 the same). Think-aloud: "Same perimeter means the same fence. I find the fence of the rectangle, then share it equally among the 4 sides of the square." Point out the link to teach 1: the square has the bigger area.

p3l7-ws1.note: Minutes 43 to 57. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. Q1: check children count edges, not squares, for the perimeter, and push out where they can (B is a staircase). Q2: "What do length and width add up to?" (9). PAGE 1 CLOCK (43 to 57): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 10.5 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l7-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: B pushes out to a 5 by 2 rectangle: 5 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 14. D has a dent: pushing out gives a 3 by 2 rectangle (10 cm), plus the 2 walls of the dent: 12 cm. Q1b is surprising: three very different figures, one perimeter. Q2: length + width = 9. Q3: 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20, 20 ÷ 4 = 5. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and hold the corrected page up to the camera once. Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l7-ws2.note: Children work alone (page 2 has no teaching slide in front of it for Q6; Q6 is if time). Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Q4: check the missing sides first (take away). Q6b has only one answer: ask "How many sides must the new square touch?"

p3l7-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q4: 10 − 6 = 4 and 7 − 4 = 3. Area: 6 × 7 + 4 × 4 = 42 + 16 = 58, or 10 × 7 − 4 × 3 = 70 − 12 = 58. Perimeter: push the step out: 10 + 7 + 10 + 7 = 34. Q5: pushing out the steps gives the 4 by 4 square, so filling it in does not change the perimeter; 16 − 10 = 6 more squares. Q6: the only empty square touching 2 sides of the L is the one to the right of the middle square. For 8 cm the new square would need to touch 3 sides: there is no gap like that. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and hold the corrected page up to the camera once. Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l7-stretch.note: For children who choose Think harder. Answers: 1) 16 by 1 (34 cm), 8 by 2 (20 cm), 4 by 4 (16 cm): the 4 by 4 square has the shortest perimeter. 2) Side 32 ÷ 4 = 8 cm, so each rectangle is 8 cm by 4 cm: perimeter 24 cm. 3) For example a 2 by 4 rectangle with one corner square missing, or a 3 by 3 square with two corners missing (corners pushed out: still 12 cm). Squeeze the squares together as much as you can.

p3l7-challenge.note: SUPPORT FOR Q6 (if time; this replaces the old add-one-square slide), only for a child who chooses it: start with an L of 3 squares (perimeter 8 cm). A new square brings 4 new edges, and every side it touches hides 2 edges: touching 1 side adds 2 cm, touching 2 sides changes nothing, touching 3 sides takes away 2 cm. Use as a pair challenge or in talk time. Ask for the reason every time. Answers: 1) Biggest 24 cm (12 edges of 2 cm, e.g. a row of 5); smallest 20 cm (10 edges: a 2 by 2 square with one more square on a side). 2) Area 35 − 4 = 31 cm². Perimeter 24 cm, the same as before. More are in the question bank.

p3l7-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? Which heuristic could help: push out, or count the touching sides? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p3l7-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: 5 squares joined need at least 4 touches, so at most 20 − 8 = 12 edges. The most touches we can get is 5 (a 2 by 2 block uses 4 touches, the fifth square adds 1), so at least 20 − 10 = 10 edges. Each edge is 2 cm. Q2: cutting a corner square out takes away area but the two new edges are just the old edges pushed in, so the perimeter does not change.

p3l7-talk.note: Minutes 72 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: No. A 9 m by 1 m garden and a 5 m by 5 m garden both have a 20 m fence, but the areas are 9 m² and 25 m². Follow-up: "When does pushing out the steps NOT work?" (When the shape has a dent: the walls of the dent are extra.) Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l7-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: 8 cm². Length + width = 12 ÷ 2 = 6, so the width is 2 cm; 4 × 2 = 8. Children who write 48 multiplied 12 × 4; children who write 8 cm found the width as 12 − 4. Extension: find all the rectangles with whole-cm sides and a perimeter of 24 cm. Which has the biggest area? (6 rectangles; 6 by 6, 36 cm²) Answers are shown only to the tutor on camera (own paper). Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l7-reflect.note: Minutes 85 to 88. Look back: short and safe. SAY: "Turn to the last page of today and find Look back. Tick or write one thing for each line. There are no right answers, and you may pass on any line." Give the children a full 2 minutes, then a short share (the slide has 3 minutes). The page is never collected, marked or read out in front of the group. Children keep their page. The tutor does not see the page, so say: "If something is still puzzling you, you can show this page to a grown-up at home, or tell me at the start of next lesson." At the start of the next lesson, in the open session, invite anyone who would like another look at a puzzle (volunteers only, by hand signal or in the chat; never a private message). Invite volunteers only (one or two) to share something they did well, or what helped. Praise the strategy ("you drew it and that got you unstuck"), not the speed or the answer. Then stamp the journal and close (minutes 88 to 90).
